hero.title: Weight Loss Chart and Log Template
hero.lead:
A list of weights is not a chart. A chart is a list plus two things: context for each reading, and a weekly average that filters the noise. Without those, you're reading each number as a verdict.

Below: a template to copy, a weekly summary block, and how to pull a real trend from data that swings 1-2 kg (2-4 lb) a day for reasons unrelated to fat.

sections.heading: What to record at every weigh-in
sections.html:
• Date - weigh at a consistent time, ideally first thing.
  • Weight - exactly as displayed, no rounding. Pick kg or lbs; never switch mid-log.
  • Notes - the column that does the real work: salty meal, hard workout, poor sleep, travel, alcohol, illness, day of cycle. Where every unexplained jump gets explained.

Worth adding: weekly waist circumference - it often keeps moving when the scale doesn't (see waist-to-height ratio) - and daily steps, because everyday movement falls silently during a diet.

Record immediately: numbers written an hour later drift toward what you hoped for.

sections.heading: The log template
sections.html:
One row per weigh-in:

DateWeightWaistNotes
Mon 3 Aug84.2 kg92 cmBaseline
Tue 4 Aug84.6 kg Restaurant dinner, salty
Wed 5 Aug83.9 kg -
Thu 6 Aug83.7 kg -
Fri 7 Aug84.1 kg First gym session in months
Sat 8 Aug84.4 kg Late night, two drinks
Sun 9 Aug83.8 kg -
    

Look at the week whole: readings bounce between 83.7 and 84.6 - a 0.9 kg spread - yet every high day has its explanation in the notes. Any single row tells a different story than the week.

Weigh under the same conditions every time; how often is its own decision - see how often you should weigh yourself.

sections.heading: The weekly summary block
sections.html:
This smaller table is where progress appears. One row each Sunday: average the week's readings, compare to last week.

WeekAverageChange% of body weightNotes
1 (3-9 Aug)84.1 kg--Baseline week
2 (10-16 Aug)83.4 kg-0.7 kg0.8%Good adherence
3 (17-23 Aug)83.2 kg-0.2 kg0.2%Traveling, poor sleep
4 (24-30 Aug)82.6 kg-0.6 kg0.7%Back to routine
     

Four weeks, 1.5 kg down, about 0.5% of body weight per week - inside the safe range of 0.5-1 kg (1-2 lb) per week. Week 3 looks bad and isn't - it's a normal week with a travel note. Anyone reading only the daily log spent it convinced the plan had stopped.

Keep the percentage column - it stays meaningful as you lighten and says whether you're going too fast.

sections.heading: How to read a trend from noisy data
sections.html:
Water, glycogen, gut content, hormones and salt each move the scale more in a day than fat does in a week (sizes in why your weight fluctuates daily). Three rules do the work:

  1. Never compare two days - compare week to week, or this week's average to three weeks ago; single days measure water.
  2. Expect a staircase, not a slope. Two good weeks, a flat one, a small rise, a drop. Treating the flat week as failure is why people quit working plans.
  3. Use three to four flat weeks as your threshold. Below that, do nothing; past it, work through how to break a weight loss plateau.

Drawing by hand? Readings as dots, a line through each week's cluster - dots are weather, the line is climate. Don't scale the axis to the last two weeks: give it 10 kg, or a chart from 82 to 85 kg turns fluctuation into a mountain range.

sections.heading: Charting more than weight
sections.html:
The scale measures one thing badly and misses several entirely: if you're training, muscle gained offsets fat lost while your body visibly changes. Three additions fix that:

  • Waist, weekly. Same spot, same tape, morning. It frequently keeps falling through a scale plateau.
  • Photos, monthly. Same lighting, position, clothing. Nobody trusts them now; everybody finds them convincing three months later.
  • How clothes fit. Unmeasurable, and often the first honest signal. Write it in the notes.

Optionally add body fat percentage: home methods aren't precise, but a consistent one shows a direction.

sections.heading: Notebook, spreadsheet, or app: an honest comparison
sections.html:
The template is complete: a notebook and a Sunday-evening average will run it for a year - if that's what you'll stick with, go rule some columns. A spreadsheet averages and charts for you.

Both cost upkeep, and upkeep is where logs die: averaging seven numbers every Sunday is the two-minute chore people skip in week three - and once averaging stops, the log stops meaning anything. Weight Journal Feeltracker is free and removes that step: averages and trend lines computed for you; charts over any period; weight, BMI and body fat in one entry, kg or lbs, with goal tracking; photos on entries; reminders, widgets, Apple Health sync so a smart scale fills the log for you; export to PDF, XLSX, CSV or JSON; and iCloud sync with no account or email - plus AI insights in the free tier.

Paper, spreadsheet or app: record consistently, judge weekly, never argue with one morning. The log you keep beats the perfect one you abandon.

items.question: What should a weight loss chart include?
items.answer: Date, weight and a **notes** column at minimum - the notes make an unexplained jump explainable. Add a weekly summary row with the week's average, the change from last week, and that change as a percentage of body weight. Waist measurement and photos are the most valuable optional additions.

items.question: How do I work out my weekly average?
items.answer: Add the week's readings and divide by how many you took - missing days are fine, just don't average a two-reading week against a seven-reading one. Compare averages week to week, never day to day, because [daily fluctuation](/weight/weight-fluctuation/) is far larger than a week's real progress.

items.question: How often should I update my chart?
items.answer: Log every time you weigh, and update the weekly summary once a week on a fixed day. Daily weighing gives the most reliable trend line; two to three times a week is a good middle ground. Avoid Monday as your summary day - the weekend's food and salt are usually still with you.

items.question: My chart is flat for two weeks. What now?
items.answer: Nothing yet. Two flat weeks is well within normal fluctuation, especially after new exercise or in the second half of a menstrual cycle. Use **three to four flat weeks** as the threshold, then work through [how to break a weight loss plateau](/weight/weight-loss-plateau/).

items.question: Should I chart in kg or pounds?
items.answer: Whichever you think in - just never switch mid-log, since a change of units makes the whole history unreadable. Either way, add the percentage-of-body-weight column: it stays meaningful as you get lighter.

data.disclaimerText: This article is for general information only and is not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. A personal log supports, but never replaces, professional care - talk to your doctor or a registered dietitian before starting a weight loss plan, particularly if you are pregnant, under 18, or managing a medical condition. See a doctor if you are losing weight without trying, particularly more than about 5% of your body weight over 6-12 months. If keeping a weight log is causing distress, becoming compulsive, or driving restrictive eating, please stop and speak to a qualified professional.
